author: TIMOTHY A. FARWELL
title: Pickleball, sweat and Southern hospitality - NewsBreak
text:
By TIMOTHY A. FARWELL ,
7 hours ago I recently returned to my hometown of Georgetown, South Carolina — a charming little place where the sweet tea flows like water and the humidity slaps you in the face like a wet beach towel.
I had grand plans: maybe take a scenic walk on the beautiful beaches, reconnect with nature, contemplate life while swatting mosquitoes. You know, the usual vacation stuff.
But before I could even lace up my sneakers or Google “activities that don’t involve sweating profusely,” my 82-year-old aunt — who, by the way, has more energy than a toddler on a cup cake — asked me the most unexpected question: “Wanna play pickleball?”
It’s that sport that sounds like a snack and looks like tennis, ping pong and badminton had a love child. Naturally, I said yes. I mean, how often do you get invited to join a geriatric free for all?
We played at two locations: the Georgetown public park and an elementary school gym. Let me paint the picture. The park had tennis courts that were clearly designed in the 1800s and hadn’t seen a tennis ball since the Clinton administration. The pickleball lines were painted over the tennis lines, which were painted over the ghost of some long-forgotten shuffleboard court. It was like playing on a Jackson Pollock painting.
The gym, on the other hand, had air conditioning. Sweet, glorious air conditioning. It also had basketball lines, volleyball lines and possibly the remnants of a hopscotch grid. The pickleball lines were in there somewhere, probably hiding behind a three-point arc and a foul line. It was like trying to play chess on a Twister mat.
But did that stop the locals? Absolutely not. These pickleball warriors came from all over the county — some driving 50 miles just to play in the cool, climate-controlled chaos of the elementary school gym. Everyone brought their own net, like pickleball MacGyvers. They set up like NASA engineers with the enthusiasm of dads grilling on Father’s Day.
And the people? Oh, the people. They were delightful. Southern charm meets competitive spirit. Every missed shot was met with a cheerful “Nice try!” and every accidental body slam into the wall was followed by “You OK, sugar?” It was like being hugged by a community wrapped in athletic tape and good intentions.
No one cared if you had to sit out. In fact, sitting out was practically a badge of honor. “You go ahead, honey,” they’d say. “I’m just here for the fellowship.” Fellowship is Southern for “sweating profusely while pretending you’re not trying to win.”
The tennis courts at the outdoor park were a sad sight — unused, unloved and probably haunted by the ghost of a forgotten P.E. teacher. They will soon be converted into pickleball courts. Anything would be better than their current status as “concrete wasteland with net poles.”
But once you got used to the crisscrossing lines and the occasional skateboarder rolling through, it was magical. The camaraderie, the laughter, the shared confusion about which line was actually in bounds — it was all part of the charm.
And here’s the kicker: it reminded me of the pickleball community back in the Upper Keys. Same warmth, same “good shot!” shouts, same willingness to welcome strangers like long-lost cousins at a family reunion. It’s like there’s a secret pickleball code: wherever you go, if you’ve got a paddle and a pulse, you’re family.
So if you’re a pickleball player and you’re traveling, don’t worry about finding a fancy court or deciphering a maze of painted lines. Just show up. Someone will hand you a paddle, shout “Nice serve!” even if you hit the wall and make you feel like you belong.
Because pickleball isn’t just a sport. It’s a movement. A sweaty, line-confused, net-dragging, joy-filled movement. And I’m proud to be part of it — even if I still don’t know which line is the baseline.
